title: The Yard Well — Low Kiln, Sill
caption: The most-named uncharted stage of the daily round, drawn at the scale of a pail set down on the stone where a pail always stands: the shared well of the low houses with its little roof, uneven curb, eleven links to the water and the twelfth that hangs dry in the hand; the white frost-bloom on the north lip where the Warm went out of the stone and the thawed edge where the sun took it off; the trough skinned bare and the silt-clouded plate of ice set on the flat stone out of the path of feet. At the bucket-round a woman draws with the pail against her knee and her hand toward her sleeve, the count kept in wood and unread, while a man brings a number up out of a shut fist toward the well and puts it back, so the figure arrives nowhere. The slate lies open on the lip with the writing turned toward its owner and nobody reading it aloud; the words spoken to the boards and the well-roof stand at five shapings with no owner standing under them, and the two tellings of the counting room shut in the last war do not touch. The Vail kiln-house, House Silt and the birth-flower shrine lie faint to the west, the drying racks to the east with the space under the lowest gone around, the Clay Road running west to the Cross and east the eighteen leagues to Greybank, High Kiln over the terrace above, the clay-heavy Slip Brook and the Ilm among the reedbeds below. Cartouche dated Y.H. 814, the month of Ilmen, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the water that tasted different, the number that is kept back, the pail that goes down into weather and the plate of ice standing where the weather was told to stand. An engraved pail on a well-chain sits in the margin.
